name: May 1998 Storm & Radiation Belt Enhancement

phenomena.details: Severe geomagnetic storm with Dst ~ −205 nT (May 4 main phase of a two-step storm) during the ascending phase of Solar Cycle 23, followed by an exceptional weeks-long relativistic-electron enhancement and a transient new radiation belt.
M-class flare activity preceding the storm.
CME associated with the geomagnetic storm.

impacts.description: The May 4 storm produced an intense, multi-week enhancement of relativistic (>MeV) 'killer' electrons and a transient new radiation belt, sharply raising the deep-dielectric-charging hazard for satellites at GEO. The widely publicised Galaxy IV failure on May 19 occurred during this elevated-electron period, but the operator's investigation attributed it to tin-whisker short circuits in the spacecraft control processor; a space-weather contribution was hypothesised (Baker 1998) but never established.
Aurora visible at mid-latitudes during the May 4 geomagnetic storm.

papers.title: Galaxy IV – when bad things happen to good satellites
papers.keyFinding: Raised the hypothesis that the elevated relativistic-electron environment may have contributed to the Galaxy IV failure; the operator later attributed the failure to tin-whisker short circuits, and the space-weather role remains unproven.

summary: The May 4, 1998 geomagnetic storm (Dst ~ −205 nT) and its exceptional weeks-long relativistic-electron enhancement created a transient new radiation belt and a sustained satellite-charging hazard. The famous Galaxy IV pager-satellite failure two weeks later is often linked to this period but was officially attributed to tin whiskers, not space weather.
description: In early May 1998, during the ascending phase of Solar Cycle 23, a two-step geomagnetic storm peaked on May 4 with Dst ~ −205 nT. The storm drove an exceptional enhancement of relativistic (>MeV) electrons in the outer magnetosphere and produced a transient new radiation belt that kept the 'killer electron' environment elevated for roughly six weeks – a sustained internal-charging hazard for geostationary satellites. The period is best known for the PanAmSat Galaxy IV failure on May 19, which knocked out roughly 80% of US pagers (about 45 million) and disrupted broadcast and data feeds, making it one of the most publicly visible satellite failures of the era. However, the failure occurred about two weeks after the storm peak, and the manufacturer's investigation attributed it to tin-whisker short circuits in the spacecraft control processor rather than to the space environment; the space-weather contribution, raised by Baker (1998), was never established. The episode is notable both as a genuine extreme relativistic-electron event and as a cautionary case in the difficulty of attributing satellite anomalies.
